sentences.text: Monday morning at Contoso.
A maker builds an HR agent and, to test faster, switches authentication to No authentication.
Then the link gets shared.
Now anyone with that link can chat with an agent that knows HR policies.
Who should have stopped this?
Copilot Studio has two safety nets, and admins have tools to govern hundreds of agents at once.
By the end of this class you will know exactly which one stops what.
Here is the picture to keep.
The security scan is an alarm.
It rings when you weaken a setting, but you can still walk through the door.
A data policy is a guard.
The administrator posts it at the door, and it simply does not let you pass.
One warns, the other prevents.
Many governance questions on the exam come down to this difference.
Let's watch the alarm.
Our maker switches from Authenticate with Microsoft to No authentication.
The scan warns.
If tools switch from end user credentials to the maker's own credentials, it warns again.
If the agent is shared with the whole organization, it warns too, because by default an agent is shared with nobody.
Notice the pattern.
Each warning means a default was weakened.
And notice the limit: the maker can still publish.
Now the guard.
The administrator defines data policies in Power Platform, for each environment.
A data policy works on connectors.
Here is the key idea: almost everything an agent does rides on a connector.
Channels, knowledge sources, tools, even M C P servers.
So when the admin blocks a connector, that capability simply disappears for every maker in the environment.
It does not warn, it blocks.
Blocked.
